scenario: AITA because I stopped giving my neighbours food? | My family lives in an apartment building. Everyone works from home at the moment so I have a lot of time to cook which is one of my passions. Our neighbours both work in a hospital, she's a doctor and he's a nurse. So I asked them if they would like some food and they said yes. So the last few weeks I always froze heaps of food and gave it to them so that every day they could just quickly heat something up. They seemed to appreciate it. Skip to last Wednesday. It was my daughter's 16th birthday and I wanted to make her favourite cake. At 1pm I started mixing all ingredients together. Only 5 minutes later I hear someone ringing our doorbell. I was our neighbour and she seemed quite upset. She said they only just got home and wanted some rest. I apologised and explained it was my daughter's birthday. She said it's selfish of me and that right now there are other things that are more important and her sleep is one of those things. I felt really bad and later brought them 2 slices of the cake as an apology. But later when I talked to my husband about it he said that yes some things are different now but that doesn't mean that our daughter's birthday is not important too. I thought about it and agreed. I haven't brought them any more food since. I do feel guilty for this and I'm not sure if I'm overreacting. AITA for how I handle this situation ?

I don't have any religious holidays or a sacred calendar — my schedule is just built around work, people I care about, and whatever I've decided actually matters to me. Do you think not having anything like that changes how someone figures out what's worth their time?

It’s a good question, and the answer depends a lot on how you’re already structuring your life. When you have a built‑in calendar—religious holidays, national observances, or even a family tradition—those dates give you a ready‑made “pause button.” They’re reminders that something else matters, that you’re part of a larger rhythm, and they can help you decide what to put on the agenda and what to let go of. If you don’t have that external framework, you’re not automatically at a disadvantage. You’re simply relying more on the *internal* cues that guide you: your values, the people you care about, the projects that excite you, and the moments that feel meaningful. In many ways, that can be a more intentional, flexible way of figuring out what’s worth your time. Here are a few ways people who don’t have a “sacred calendar” still find structure and meaning: | What you might be missing | How you can fill the gap | Why it works | |---------------------------|--------------------------|--------------| | **External reminders** | Create a personal “calendar of meaning.” Pick a few dates that feel significant—maybe the anniversary of a life‑changing event, the day you started a new job, or a seasonal marker like the first day of spring. | These dates become your own rituals, giving you a built‑in pause to reflect. | | **Community rituals** | Join a club, a sports league, or a volunteer group that meets regularly. | The regularity of a shared activity gives you a rhythm and a sense of belonging. | | **Personal milestones** | Set yearly or quarterly goals that align with your values (e.g., “read 12 books,” “learn a new skill,” “spend a weekend with my sister”). | Achieving these milestones gives you a sense of progress and purpose. | | **Nature’s rhythm** | Pay attention to the seasons, sunrise/sunset, or the changing light in your home. | Nature’s cycles can be a quiet, non‑religious reminder that time moves and that you’re part of something larger. | | **Mindful rituals** | Start a daily or weekly ritual that matters to you—morning coffee with a journal, a Sunday walk, a Friday “no‑work” evening. | Rituals anchor your day and give you a consistent way to honor yourself and others. | ### How not having a sacred calendar can change your decision‑making 1. **More intentionality** Without a pre‑set calendar, you’re forced to ask yourself, “What do I want to do today?” and “Why does this matter?” That can sharpen your focus on what truly aligns with your values. 2. **Greater flexibility** You’re not tied to a fixed schedule of obligations. That can be liberating, especially if you’re juggling unpredictable work demands or caring for people who need you. 3. **Risk of “time‑suck”** On the flip side, without external prompts, it’s easier to let the day slip by or to get lost in low‑value tasks. That’s why many people who don’t have a built‑in calendar find it helpful to set up a simple system—like a “priority list” or a “time‑block” calendar—to keep themselves on track. 4. **Personal meaning over communal meaning** Your calendar will be more about *you* than about a shared tradition. That can be deeply satisfying if you’re someone who values autonomy and self‑definition. ### Practical steps to build your own “sacred” structure 1. **Identify your core values** Write down the top 3–5 things that matter most to you (e.g., health, learning, relationships, creativity). These will be the compass for your calendar. 2. **Choose a few anchor dates** Pick 3–5 dates that feel significant—maybe the day you graduated, the day you met your partner, or a seasonal marker. Mark them on your calendar and commit to doing something special on those days. 3. **Create a ritual list** List 5–10 rituals that you can do regularly (daily, weekly, monthly). They don’t have to be elaborate—just something that signals a pause or a celebration. 4. **Use a simple planning tool** A physical planner, a digital calendar, or a habit‑tracking app can help you see your commitments at a glance. Color‑code your values so you can quickly spot whether your day is balanced. 5. **Reflect regularly** Set aside a weekly or monthly review. Ask: “Did I spend my time on what matters?” “What could I shift next month?” This reflection turns your calendar into a living, evolving guide. ### Bottom line Not having a religious or communal calendar doesn’t mean you can’t figure out what’s worth your time. It just means you’ll be doing it in a more self‑directed way. Many people find that this autonomy leads to a richer sense of purpose, because every decision is a deliberate choice aligned with their own values. If you ever feel adrift, try creating a few personal anchor points and rituals—your own “sacred calendar” that’s entirely yours.
